harrison.pages: Harrison 22e, Chap. 290 (Deep-Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism), p.2155-2164; Chap. 69 (Bleeding and Thrombosis) p.473-474; Chap. 98 (Cancer and venous thrombosis) p.~705; Chap. 27 (d-Dimer) p.~158
clinicalPearls: The classic DVT symptom is a calf cramp or 'charley horse' that persists and worsens over several days, rather than a sudden event (Harrison 22e p.2159).
A diffusely edematous (whole-leg) limb actually makes ordinary DVT less likely, with the important exception of phlegmasia cerulea dolens, the most severe form of DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159).

Recurrent left thigh edema, especially in a young woman, should raise suspicion of May-Thurner syndrome, in which the right common iliac artery compresses the left common iliac vein and may precipitate DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159).

Upper extremity DVT may show only subtle asymmetry of the supraclavicular fossa or upper-arm circumference; it is increasingly linked to PICC lines and rises with larger catheter diameter and more lumens (Harrison 22e p.2158-2159, 2161).
Superficial vein thrombosis presents with erythema, tenderness and a palpable cord and carries a risk of extension into the deep venous system (Harrison 22e p.2158).
An idiopathic (no clear precipitant) VTE is the strongest predictor of recurrence in patients without malignancy (Harrison 22e p.473).
Testing for inherited thrombophilia in adults should be reserved for the rare situation where the result would actually change management (Harrison 22e p.473-474).
harrison.pathophysiology: DVT arises from Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury, now understood to be typically coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Activated platelets release proinflammatory microparticles that recruit neutrophils to form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); these histone-rich, web-like networks promote platelet aggregation and platelet-dependent thrombin generation. Thrombi form and propagate in an environment of stasis, low oxygen tension and upregulated proinflammatory genes. Lower-extremity thrombi usually begin in the calf veins and can propagate proximally to the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; detached thrombi embolize through the vena cava and right heart into the pulmonary circulation, and rarely cross a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect to cause paradoxical (arterial) embolism. VTE shares inflammation, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury with arterial atherothrombosis, so VTE patients have more than double the risk of future MI or stroke and vice versa. Common genetic prothrombotic states are factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C) and the prothrombin gene mutation (raised prothrombin level); deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C and protein S also predispose but are rare; antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia causing both venous and arterial thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2156-2158).
additionalDifferentials: Ruptured Baker's cyst (sudden severe calf discomfort) (Harrison 22e p.2159)
Acute postthrombotic syndrome / chronic venous insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2159)
May-Thurner syndrome (iliac vein compression) presenting as recurrent leg edema (Harrison 22e p.2159)
infectionMimics: Cellulitis - fever and chills more often herald cellulitis than DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159)
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic venous insufficiency / postthrombotic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2156, 2159)
additionalInvestigations: Loss of vein compressibility is the primary ultrasound criterion for DVT; a normal vein collapses (a 'wink') under gentle transducer pressure, whereas an acutely thrombosed vein stays distended and may show central, homogeneous, low-echogenicity thrombus (Harrison 22e p.2160).
Doppler interrogation adds flow data: calf compression normally augments flow, and loss of respiratory variation suggests an obstructing DVT or a pelvic obstructive process (Harrison 22e p.2160).
Contrast (gadolinium) MR venography is an excellent option when pelvic or leg ultrasound is equivocal or technically nondiagnostic (Harrison 22e p.2160-2161).
Contrast phlebography is now reserved mainly for when an interventional procedure is planned (Harrison 22e p.2161).
An age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff (age x 10 ng/mL in patients >50 years) is endorsed for ruling out PE but does NOT apply to suspected acute DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159-2160).
d-Dimer rarely helps in hospitalized patients because levels are frequently elevated by systemic illness (MI, pneumonia, sepsis, cancer, postoperative state, pregnancy) (Harrison 22e p.2159).
redFlags: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens - massive proximal DVT with a diffusely swollen, painful, cyanotic limb, the most serious form of DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159).

Signs of pulmonary embolism (unexplained breathlessness, syncope, hypotension, cyanosis) since DVT can embolize; many PE patients have no detectable residual DVT because the leg clot has already embolized (Harrison 22e p.2158-2159).
Active malignancy as the underlying driver - up to ~15% of patients who develop DVT have cancer, and unprovoked VTE may be its first manifestation (Harrison 22e p.~705).
harrison.prognosis: Postthrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency) is the main long-term morbidity: damaged venous valves cause ankle/calf swelling and leg aching after prolonged standing, and in its most severe form deep skin ulceration near the medial malleolus. Notably, graduated compression stockings prescribed for asymptomatic newly diagnosed acute DVT do NOT prevent postthrombotic syndrome (they are used only for symptomatic swelling relief). Recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation is stratified (ESC 2019) as low (<3%/yr, e.g., major surgery/trauma), intermediate (3-8%/yr, e.g., minor surgery, hospitalization for acute illness, pregnancy/estrogen, long-haul flight, IBD, autoimmune disease, or no identifiable risk factor) and high (>8%/yr, active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome). Harrison de-emphasizes the 'provoked vs unprovoked' dichotomy because many provoked VTEs recur at rates similar to unprovoked ones, and enduring risk factors (heart failure, chronic lung disease, IBD) raise recurrence risk. The Post-VTE Functional Status scale (grades 0-4) can track functional recovery (Harrison 22e p.2156-2157, 2163).
pitfalls: Not all leg pain is DVT - sudden severe calf pain may be a ruptured Baker's cyst, and fever/chills point more to cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.2159).
Wells point-score rules are validated in ambulatory but NOT in hospitalized patients (Harrison 22e p.2159).
Using d-dimer to rule out DVT in hospitalized or systemically ill patients is futile because it is frequently elevated by non-thrombotic illness (Harrison 22e p.2159).
The age-adjusted d-dimer threshold validated for PE does not extend to suspected acute DVT (Harrison 22e p.2160).
In cancer patients, elevated d-dimer is far less predictive of DVT than in patients without cancer (Harrison 22e p.~705).
IVC filters can paradoxically increase the DVT rate by acting as a nidus for clot, and may still let small-to-medium clots pass via collateral veins (Harrison 22e p.2163).
Warfarin (not a DOAC) is the standard anticoagulant for antiphospholipid syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2163).
harrison.severityClassification: Wells clinical prediction rule for DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159): low likelihood if score <=0, moderate if 1-2, high if >=3. Points: active cancer +1; paralysis/paresis or recent cast +1; bedridden >3 days or major surgery <12 weeks +1; tenderness along distribution of deep veins +1; entire-leg swelling +1; unilateral calf swelling >3 cm +1; pitting edema +1; collateral superficial nonvaricose veins +1; alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT -2. Pretest-probability strategy: patients with low DVT likelihood undergo d-dimer first and need no imaging if it is normal, whereas high-likelihood patients should skip d-dimer and proceed straight to compression ultrasound imaging.
